title: New Names and the Sign in the Flesh
summary: Thirteen years after Ishmael's birth, God appears to ninety-nine-year-old Abram as God Almighty, renames him Abraham, and confirms an everlasting covenant: many nations, kings, the land of Canaan, and God himself as their God. God gives circumcision as the covenant's sign, renames Sarai as Sarah, and promises that she will bear a son named Isaac within a year. Abraham laughs, pleads for Ishmael, and then circumcises every male in his household that same day.
story: Genesis 16 ended with Abram at eighty-six and a son by Hagar. Thirteen silent years follow. Abraham may well have assumed Ishmael was the promised heir. Now God speaks again and makes clear that the covenant will run through a son of Sarah, not the son of the slave woman's arrangement. The covenant first cut in Genesis 15 is here widened and given a visible sign that every generation of Israel will carry. From here on, the story will move toward the birth of Isaac (Genesis 21), and the names Abraham and Sarah will stand for the promise itself.
historical:
Circumcision was not invented in Genesis 17. It was practiced in Egypt long before Israel existed; a tomb relief at Saqqara from around 2300 BC depicts the operation. Jeremiah 9:25-26 names Egypt, Edom, Ammon, and Moab among circumcised peoples, while the Philistines, who came from the Aegean world, were notably uncircumcised. What set Israel's practice apart was its timing and its meaning. Elsewhere circumcision was commonly performed around puberty or before marriage; Israel's sons were circumcised on the eighth day, as infants, and the act marked belonging to God's covenant rather than coming of age. Ishmael, circumcised at thirteen (verse 25), follows a different pattern, and the Jewish historian Josephus, writing in the first century AD, noted that the Arabs of his own day circumcised boys at thirteen because Ishmael had been.

As with earlier chapters, the date of Abraham depends on how one reads the patriarchal narratives; those who take them as history generally place him early in the second millennium BC.
cultural:
Names in the ancient world carried identity and destiny, and a superior's power to rename someone signaled authority over them; Pharaoh renames Joseph (Genesis 41:45) and Nebuchadnezzar's official renames Daniel (Daniel 1:7). Here God renames Abram (usually understood as exalted father) as Abraham, which the text explains by a play on the Hebrew for father of a multitude. Sarai becomes Sarah; both forms mean princess, and the change marks a new stage rather than a new meaning. The promise that kings will come from both of them (verses 6 and 16) points ahead to Israel's monarchy.

The covenant sign was cut into the body of every male in the household, including slaves bought from foreigners (verses 12-13). This meant that belonging to Abraham's covenant family was never purely a matter of bloodline. The penalty for refusing it, being “cut off from his people” (verse 14), plays on the language of cutting a covenant: the one who refuses the cut is himself cut off.
literary: The chapter is built almost entirely of God's speech, with brief narrative frames. The word covenant occurs thirteen times, more than in any other chapter of Genesis. God speaks in a series of addresses, each introduced by a formula: what God will do (verses 4-8), what Abraham must do (verses 9-14), and what God will do for Sarah (verses 15-16). Abraham falls facedown twice (verses 3 and 17), once in worship and once in laughter. The phrase “everlasting covenant”, first used of the covenant with Noah (9:16), is joined here to the formula “to be your God”, a pairing that will echo through the prophets. The chapter ends with a careful account of obedience: “On that very day” Abraham does exactly what God said.

outline.t: Abraham, father of many nations, and the everlasting covenant
Circumcision, the sign of the covenant
Sarah renamed and Isaac promised; Ishmael blessed
Abraham circumcises his household that day

doctrines.note: God confirms the covenant as “an everlasting covenant” and gives it a sign. At its heart is the promise “to be your God and the God of your descendants after you” (verse 7), the core of every later covenant, which Revelation 21:3 echoes at the Bible's end.

Circumcision is the first covenant sign carried in the body, a visible mark of an invisible promise. Christians later reflected on how it relates to baptism (see the hard question). Scripture also insists that the outward sign must be matched by an inward reality (Deuteronomy 10:16; Jeremiah 4:4).

God introduces himself as God Almighty and calls Abraham to “Walk before Me and be blameless” (verse 1). The God who can give a son to a man of a hundred and a woman of ninety is the one who sets the terms of the relationship.

words.note: Shaddai, usually translated Almighty. Its origin is uncertain. Proposals include a link with a verb meaning to overpower, with an Akkadian word for mountain, and with the Hebrew word for breast, which fits the name's frequent setting in promises of fruitfulness (Genesis 28:3; 49:25). Exodus 6:3 says this was the name by which God was known to the patriarchs.

Tamim, whole, complete, blameless. Used of sacrificial animals without defect, and of Noah (Genesis 6:9). It doesn't mean sinless perfection, as Abraham's story shows, but wholehearted integrity before God.

Ot, sign. A visible mark pointing to something beyond itself. The rainbow was the sign of God's covenant with Noah (Genesis 9:12-13); the Sabbath will be a sign of the Sinai covenant (Exodus 31:13). Circumcision is the sign carried in the body of each male of the covenant family.

Tsachaq, to laugh. Abraham laughs at the thought of a son at a hundred (verse 17), and the promised son is named Isaac, which means he laughs. Whether Abraham's laugh was joy, disbelief, or both is debated; Sarah will laugh too (18:12), and at Isaac's birth she will speak of laughter again (21:6).

christ: Paul uses this chapter in Romans 4:9-12 to point out that Abraham was counted righteous in Genesis 15, before he was circumcised in Genesis 17, so that circumcision was “a seal of the righteousness” he already had by faith, and he is father to believers who are uncircumcised as well as those who are. The promise that Abraham would be “the father of many nations” (verse 4) is quoted in Romans 4:17 and read as fulfilled in the gathering of Gentiles into God's people through Christ. Jesus himself was circumcised on the eighth day (Luke 2:21), fully inside this covenant. Colossians 2:11-12 speaks of “the circumcision performed by Christ and not by human hands” that believers receive in him, linked to being buried with him in baptism. And the kings promised to Abraham and Sarah lead to David and to the King descended from him.

hard.q: Does circumcision given to infants in Genesis 17 mean that baptism should be given to infants?
hard.a:
This is one of the church's long-standing second-order disagreements, and faithful Christians land on both sides. Those who baptize infants, including the Roman Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican, Presbyterian, and Reformed traditions (often with different theological reasons), point to the continuity of God's covenant with believers and their children. Circumcision was given to infants who could not yet believe, as a sign of God's promise, and Colossians 2:11-12 links circumcision and baptism; Acts 2:39 says the promise is for you and your children, and Acts records whole households being baptized.

Those who baptize only believers who profess faith, including Baptist, many free-church, and Pentecostal traditions, stress what is new in the new covenant. Jeremiah 31:31-34 promises a covenant in which all its members will know the LORD, so the sign should follow a profession of faith. In the New Testament, baptism is consistently tied to repentance and belief, and Paul's point in Romans 4 is that Abraham's faith came before his sign. Both sides agree that the covenant rests on God's promise, not human merit, though they differ on what the sign itself conveys.

questions: Abraham had waited twenty-four years since the first promise. What does it do to faith to wait that long, and what sustains it?
God gave a new name with the renewed promise. How does the way God names us differ from the names others give us or we give ourselves?
Abraham asked God to bless Ishmael, and God did. What does the chapter show about God's care for those outside the main line of the story?
